title: Water Survival & Purification
description: A modular field guide for finding, collecting, clarifying, filtering, disinfecting, desalinating and storing water.

articles.title: Emergency Water Storage at Home
articles.summary: Prepare a household reserve in clean, food-grade containers and keep untreated water separate from treated drinking water.
articles.body: A household water reserve reduces dependence on continuous municipal supply. Store water in purpose-made food-grade containers, keep them sealed, and protect them from heat, sunlight, chemicals and physical damage.
steps: Wash hands and clean the container and cap.
Sanitize reusable containers using an approved drinking-water container procedure.
Fill with safe drinking water and seal the container.
Label the water source and storage date.
Store in a cool, dark place away from fuels, pesticides and cleaning chemicals.
Inspect periodically and replace self-filled stored water according to public-health guidance.
safety: Never reuse containers that held chemicals, fuel, pesticides or non-food substances.
Keep raw and treated water physically separated.
Do not assume a container is food-grade from appearance alone.
limitations: Storage does not make contaminated water safe.
Heat, sunlight and dirty dispensing methods can compromise stored water.

articles.title: Cloth Pre-Filtration for Muddy Water
articles.summary: Clean cloth can remove visible debris and larger particles as a preliminary step; it does not disinfect water.
articles.body: Cloth filtration is a clarification step, not a complete water-treatment method. It may reduce visible particles, but pathogens and dissolved chemicals can remain.
steps: Allow very muddy water to settle first where practical.
Fold clean cloth into several layers.
Secure it over a clean receiving container.
Pour water slowly without disturbing settled sediment.
Repeat with a clean section of cloth if visible particles remain.
Follow with an appropriate disinfection method for microbiological risks.
safety: Cloth filtration does not reliably remove bacteria, viruses, protozoa, salts or chemical contaminants.
Do not use cloth filtration to make floodwater, sewage-contaminated water or chemically polluted water drinkable.
limitations: Performance varies with cloth weave and water turbidity.
This is only a pre-treatment step.

articles.title: Rolling Boil for Microbiological Safety
articles.summary: Boiling kills disease-causing microorganisms, but does not remove dissolved salts, heavy metals or most chemical pollutants.
articles.body: Bring water to a rolling boil. Follow current public-health guidance for altitude and duration. Let it cool naturally in a clean, covered container.
steps: If water is cloudy, let it settle and filter it through a clean cloth or suitable pre-filter.
Bring water to a rolling boil.
Maintain the boil for the duration specified by current public-health guidance for the location and altitude.
Allow water to cool without adding untreated water or ice.
Store in a clean, covered container.
safety: Boiling does not remove salt, fuel, pesticides, heavy metals or radioactive contaminants.
Some chemical contaminants can become more concentrated as water evaporates.
Use caution around open flames and hot vessels.
limitations: Not suitable as a remedy for chemically contaminated or saline water.

articles.title: Rainwater Harvesting with First-Flush Diversion
articles.summary: Collect roof runoff using gutters and a covered tank; divert the initial runoff to reduce accumulated roof debris.
articles.body: Rainwater harvesting can provide a supplementary source during supply interruptions. Roof materials and local pollution affect suitability. First-flush diversion reduces some accumulated debris but does not guarantee chemical or microbiological safety.
steps: Check that the roof and gutter materials are appropriate for collecting water.
Clean the roof and gutter before the rainy period.
Install a gutter and screened downpipe.
Add and maintain a correctly sized first-flush diverter.
Direct later runoff into a covered, opaque tank.
Use treatment appropriate to the intended use and contamination risks; test where chemical contamination is possible.
safety: Do not collect drinking water from roofs containing asbestos, lead-based coatings or other hazardous materials.
First flush is not a substitute for disinfection or chemical testing.
Protect tanks from insects and animal access.
limitations: Yield varies with rainfall, catchment area and losses.
Urban air pollution and roofing materials can affect quality.

articles.title: Seawater Desalination by Distillation
articles.summary: Distillation evaporates water and condenses the vapour, leaving most dissolved salts behind. Improvised systems must remain pressure-safe.
articles.body: A purpose-designed distillation setup can produce freshwater from seawater. The vapour path and condenser must use suitable materials, and the apparatus must not be sealed without engineered pressure relief.
steps: Use a purpose-designed, pressure-safe distillation apparatus.
Keep seawater in the boiling chamber and separate the freshwater collection side.
Heat the seawater so vapour enters the condenser.
Cool vapour in the condenser and collect condensate in a clean vessel.
Inspect for leaks, material degradation and saltwater carry-over.
Use appropriate testing if the source may contain volatile industrial chemicals or fuel.
safety: Never seal a boiling vessel without a properly designed pressure-relief path.
Do not use unknown plastics, solder, coatings or metals in the vapour or condensate path.
Distillation may not remove volatile contaminants; do not distil chemically polluted seawater.
limitations: Requires fuel or power and a suitable condenser.
Output depends on apparatus and energy input.

articles.title: Solar Still for Small-Scale Water Recovery
articles.summary: A solar still uses solar heat to evaporate water and a transparent cover to collect condensate. Output is usually low and is not a dependable sole source.
articles.body: Solar stills can recover small quantities of water from suitable wet material or saline feed through evaporation and condensation. The system must prevent feedwater droplets from splashing into the collection cup.
steps: Choose a location with sustained direct sunlight and no nearby contamination source.
Place a clean collection cup at the lowest point.
Arrange wet feed material or saline water around the cup without splashing into it.
Seal a transparent cover and slope it toward the cup.
Keep the collection vessel clean and prevent feedwater from entering it.
Assess the condensate based on the feed source and construction materials.
safety: Do not use chemically polluted soil or water as feedstock.
Avoid plastics that may soften, degrade or leach chemicals in heat.
Solar still output is highly weather- and design-dependent.
limitations: Cloud cover, humidity and surface area affect yield.
Not a dependable sole water source.
